items.why: Strong agent contrast: the five spies enter and take the objects while the priest and soldiers remain at the gate.
Excellent chronology trap: the five men take the items first, though the priest handles them later.
The trees clearly request their own king; the gods-and-humans alternative is an incidental phrase about wine.
The passage explicitly links prosperity to the land lacking nothing, while resemblance to Sidonians concerns security.
Two nearby circumstances compete, but only the missing inheritance is explicitly given as the reason for seeking land.
Jotham’s fear is explicitly tied to Abimelek; the Shechem citizens enter the narrative only afterward.
Strong nested-recipient distinction: Abimelek addresses his maternal relatives and tells them to ask the citizens.
The text distinguishes the Levite’s purpose, finding lodging, from Micah’s house as an incidental destination en route.
The requested blessing does precede the fire curse, but calling it a request is somewhat unnatural.
The pronoun points to the Levite, but the question is awkward and the competing nearby people are not plausible recipients.
The reported news about people going to the fields must be separated from Abimelek’s later sight of them leaving the city.
Excellent role contrast: the mother says her son will make the image, but the later action assigns manufacture to a silversmith.
Grammar clearly makes Abimelek the servant’s victim, leaving little room for the proposed servant-dies reading.
The fire directly kills the occupants, whereas entering the stronghold is an earlier action that only exposes them.
Excellent duration contrast between the priests serving until captivity and the idol lasting while God’s house was at Shiloh.
The shouting immediately prompts the turn, while overtaking is a nearby prior event that can be mistaken for the trigger.
The fig tree’s stated reason is preserving its fruit; the trees’ subsequent appeal to the vine is a plausible sequence distraction.
The doorway approach has the explicit purpose of setting the tower on fire, though attacking it is also broadly true.
The pronoun’s antecedent is the land, but common conquest language makes taking over the people somewhat plausible.
The explicit 'since' clause makes the Levite’s priesthood the reason, not his previously stated hometown.
The route clearly places Ephraim immediately before Micah’s house, though the question’s wording is repetitive and stiff.
Resolving 'him' to Jerub-Baal requires preserving the family relation rather than attaching it to Abimelek.
Zebul is the explicit secret sender, while Gaal is the embedded antagonist whose words prompted the message.
Strong mediation distinction: they ask the priest to inquire, while God is the one from whom guidance is sought.
The curse does fall on the people, but 'after God punishes them' imposes an unclear chronology on a summary statement.
Zebul’s immediate correction identifies mountain shadows rather than the people Gaal claims to see.
The explicit purpose clause says their listening should lead God to listen; anointing a king belongs to the ensuing parable.
The olive tree states preserving its honoring oil as its reason; turning to the fig tree happens only afterward.
Micah’s direct address attributes the earlier curse to his mother, despite Micah being the current speaker.
The curse occurs while they eat and drink at the festival, distinctly after the earlier grape work.
The text explicitly makes isolation and lack of relationships the reason no rescuer comes, not merely the attack itself.
